title: FDA clears CorVista's AI point-of-care test for elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
subtitle: The third FDA nod for CorVista's cardiopulmonary platform lets clinicians estimate a key heart-failure indicator without an invasive catheter.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The FDA on July 28 cleared CorVista Health's AI-based add-on test for elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), a physiologic reading clinicians use to identify suspected heart failure. The test runs on CorVista's existing cardiopulmonary platform, analyzing physiologic signals captured at the point of care to produce a non-invasive PCWP assessment for patients with cardiovascular symptoms. It is meant to help distinguish heart failure with reduced ejection fraction from heart failure with preserved ejection fraction — a distinction that changes treatment.

The mechanism matters clinically because PCWP is normally measured by right-heart catheterization, an invasive procedure typically done in a cardiac cath lab. A validated non-invasive estimate at the point of care means primary care and emergency clinicians can factor PCWP into a workup earlier, potentially triaging patients to specialty care sooner and reducing the number of catheterizations done to rule the condition out. CorVista frames the AI output as augmentative — clinicians retain the diagnosis; the model provides an additional signal.

This is CorVista's third FDA clearance for the same underlying platform, following coronary artery disease in September 2023 and pulmonary hypertension in April 2024. That trajectory — one cleared cardiopulmonary sensor, extended through successive AI-driven add-ons that each get their own clearance — is becoming a common regulatory pattern for AI medical devices. Related tailwinds this month include the FDA's July 20 funding call for digital-health-technology research in drug trials and HHS's Genesis Mission AI-for-biomedicine initiative announced July 22.

For learners in health tech: the pattern to notice is platform-plus-add-ons. A single cleared hardware base plus staged AI clearances is a faster path to real deployment than trying to certify a single sprawling AI device. If you are thinking about building or evaluating clinical AI, look at what FDA has actually cleared, in what indication, and on what underlying substrate — that reveals the practical shape of the regulatory path far better than any general AI healthcare hype cycle.
